## New investigation ideas
- **[2026-11-16] The portfolio framework has one written rule for cutting AI exposure. Its price leg was met on 11-05 and 11-06 and nobody noticed, because the rule says "20% below SOXX's current level" and never records what that level was.** [[finance/models/model-portfolio-management]] (Portfolio Balance Framework) says: if two or more hyperscalers revise 2027 capex guidance down *and* SOXX falls more than 20% "from its current level", halve the AI-exposed trading positions and reassess each pension thesis. The page was created on 2026-07-27, when SOXX closed at 172.08, so the line is about 137.66. SOXX closed at 131.90 on 11-05 (−23.3%) and 136.53 on 11-06 (−20.7%), then recovered to 149.30 by 11-13 (−13.2%). Measured from its 06-22 high of 218.34 it was −39.6% on 11-05, a fraction short of the same page's AVGO invalidation line ("SOXX −40%+ sustained"). The page's weekly watch-list test, "SOXX underperforming SPY by 20%+ over 6 months", stands at 16.8 points (05-13 to 11-13: SOXX −15.2%, SPY +1.6%). All prices are Massive adjusted daily closes, checked this run. The capex leg cannot be judged from the wiki at all: no page records what Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon or Meta said about 2027 capex in their late-October reports, and SOXX's 8.2% fall on 10-30 (171.29 → 157.17) has no recorded cause. Nothing monitors either leg. [[finance/market-sector-performance]] follows SMH, not SOXX. The daily briefing covers only [[finance/trading-portfolio]]. [[finance/portfolio-overview]], the book the rule mostly protects, was last priced on 09-05. "Rebalancing trigger" appears nowhere in log.md. The 11-15 strategy-feedback proposal to rebuild the Lens 3 heat map measures AI beta; it does not check the trigger. **Next step:** (1) write the reference level (172.08, 07-27) and the 137.66 line into the rule, and say whether one close below it counts or it must hold for a set number of sessions; (2) pull the 2027 capex guidance from the four Q3 releases into one source page and mark each as raised, held or cut, which also updates [[ai-tech/data-hyperscaler-ai-revenue-2026-06-27]]; (3) add two standing lines to the Monday sector tracker: SOXX against the 137.66 line, and the 6-month SOXX-minus-SPY gap; (4) reprice the pension book, so that "reassess pension theses" starts from November prices.
- **[2026-11-16] ETH's 21% fall last week was the first real stress test of USDN, the SmarDex synthetic dollar on Fred's DeFi watchlist. It appears to have held, but the protocol holds only about $1 million.** [[crypto/company-smardex]] was written from one site clipping on 04-25 (ETH $2,318.56, 13.25% APR on the long side) and all seven of its Key Questions are still unticked, including "What is total TVL?" and "Is the 13.25% APR sustainable?". [[crypto/defi-watchlist]] has not changed since 05-01 and calls the pair "worth following closely". DefiLlama's "SMARDEX USDN" entry (category Basis Trading, sole collateral wstETH; fetched this run) shows TVL of $1.29m on 11-07 and $1.05m on 11-16, a fall of 19%. [[crypto/crypto-portfolio]] has ETH down 21.0% over nearly the same days. So the dollar fall is about what the price of the collateral explains, and little wstETH seems to have left: no run. The size is the new fact. A yield of 13% on roughly $1m of collateral says little about whether the design works at scale, and the 2026-10-11 connection below treated USDN as a serious alternative to GENIUS-Act stablecoins without knowing it. The DefiLlama figure covers the USDN protocol only, not SmarDex's DEX or lending. **Next step:** (1) tick the TVL question with this number and add the DEX's own TVL beside it; (2) pull USDN's daily price for 11-07 to 11-15 (CoinGecko) and note the largest move away from $1; (3) record the long-side APR and funding rate shown on smardex.io now, against the 04-25 clipping; (4) decide whether a $1m protocol stays on the Active Watchlist or moves to a "small / unproven" row.

## New cross-domain connections
- **[2026-11-16] AI & Tech rates Constellation Energy the most data-centre-exposed power company it tracks. Finance files Fred's holding in it as an AI-capex risk. On the day of the AI rout the stock behaved like neither: it fell less than the S&P 500 and then rallied 17%.** [[ai-tech/model-dc-power-regional-balance-2026-06-25]] gives CEG "Extreme" data-centre exposure (Microsoft, Meta and CyrusOne nuclear contracts), and [[ai-tech/data-dc-power-construction-tracker-2026-06-25]] has a whole section on it: a 60 GW fleet, and 20-year contracts for 835 MW with Microsoft and 1,100 MW with Meta. [[finance/models/model-portfolio-management]]'s heat map scores the holding 🟠 MEDIUM ("power demand collapses if AI capex slows; 18-month lag") and gives it its own ~5% "AI capex dependent" bucket. On 11-05 SOXX fell 12.1% and SPY 4.4%. CEG fell 2.5% (245.72 → 239.65), and by 11-13 it was at 280.20, 14% above its 11-04 close, while SOXX was still below its own (Massive daily closes, checked this run). [[finance/market-sector-performance]] shows utilities among the defensive leaders this quarter (XLU +11.7%). The likely reason is in the AI & Tech pages: the "exposure" is 20-year contracted revenue, so what CEG carries is the long-run credit of its hyperscaler customers, not this year's capex budgets. That makes it the one AI-linked pension holding that did not move with the AI puts in [[finance/trading-portfolio]], and neither page says so. One day is thin evidence. The other half is unexplained: [[finance/portfolio-overview]] has the entry at $482.84, so the position is about 42% under water, the AI & Tech model already had CEG's 12-month return at about −5% against Vistra's +157%, there is no idea page, and this file had never mentioned the holding. A first idea page would need to say why the best-contracted name in the power model lagged its merchant peers so badly, and whether power contracts sit inside the roughly $2.7tn of hyperscaler commitments counted in [[finance/investor-letters/source-burry-heretics-guide-part4-2026-09-19]].

0 new podcast books. No older ideas resolved.

## New investigation ideas
- **[2026-11-15] The equity portfolio holds MicroStrategy as "leveraged Bitcoin exposure". In this week's crypto fall it dropped less than Bitcoin did. Nothing in the wiki has measured how much leverage the holding still gives, and its row has not been repriced since 09-05.** [[crypto/crypto-portfolio]] (refreshed today) has BTC at $64,115, −15.4% since 11-07, which is back near the ~$60k July low described in [[crypto/source-morningstar-crypto-winter-2026-07-24]]. MSTR closed at $128.93 on 11-06 and $111.62 on 11-13 (Massive daily closes, checked this run), a fall of 13.4%. The two windows are a day apart, so the gap is approximate, but a proxy that is meant to amplify Bitcoin should have fallen clearly more, not slightly less. [[finance/portfolio-overview]] still shows MSTR at $142.80 with the note "RSI oversold; earnings Jul 30" and the thesis "Leveraged Bitcoin exposure via equity — active". The only analysis page, [[finance/technical-analysis-snapshots/technical-analysis-MSTR-2026-06-04]], is price-only ($129.35, 52-week low $104.17), and [[finance/models/model-portfolio-management]] files MSTR with BTC and ETH as one "~10%, speculative" bucket. The 07-26 connection below flagged the doubled-up exposure; it did not ask what the second leg adds. **Concrete step:** (1) regress MSTR's daily returns on BTC's from June to now, to get the actual beta; (2) from Strategy's latest 10-Q, take BTC held, average purchase cost, debt and preferred obligations, and work out the market value as a multiple of the Bitcoin it holds; (3) note whether BTC at $64k is above or below that average cost. If the beta is near 1 and the multiple is near or under 1, the holding is plain Bitcoin with a balance sheet attached, and the thesis row should say so. MSTR is about $7 above the 52-week low recorded in June, so the answer matters now. Entry was $20.45, so this is a question about what to hold from here, not about a loss.

## New cross-domain connections
- **[2026-11-15] Crypto's main source page gives two explanations for the 2026 bitcoin fall: tight macro conditions that hit all risk assets, and retail money moving out of crypto into AI. This week separates them. Crypto fell 15–21% while the AI names Fred is short went up, so his AI puts and his crypto lost money together.** [[crypto/source-morningstar-crypto-winter-2026-07-24]] calls the winter macro-driven, a retreat alongside equities, and also quotes Franklin Templeton's Perkins: "Retail risk capital has migrated toward AI". [[crypto/crypto-portfolio]] shows BTC −15.4%, ETH −21.0% and LINK −17.8% between 11-07 and 11-14. [[finance/trading-portfolio]] shows what AI did over nearly the same days (11-06 to 11-12 closes): ORCL about $116 → $127.11, PLTR about $160 → $171.58, NBIS $129.49 → $128.64 after a +15.4% day and a −16.8% day. The four daily option moves in its run notes (−€503, +€181, −€680, +€385) sum to −€617 on a put book now marked at ≈€2,125. MSTR, in [[finance/portfolio-overview]], fell 13.4%. A general risk-off week would have paid the puts while crypto fell. This week did the opposite, which fits the rotation reading. If that reading holds, the short-AI book and the long-crypto book are not two separate speculative bets, and neither hedges the other: both lose when money moves from crypto into AI. The Structural Risk Notes table in trading-portfolio has no crypto row, and [[finance/models/model-portfolio-management]] lists crypto as "not Burry's thesis; speculative" without saying which way it moves against the AI shorts. Limits: this is one week, the windows are a day apart, the crypto page keeps weekly prices only, and the midterm result logged on 11-09 is a second possible cause of a crypto-only fall. The clean test is 11-05, when the AI rout added €927 to the puts: daily BTC against SMH for October and November would show whether Bitcoin fell with AI that day or rose against it. This extends the 11-09 idea (regress the long book on SMH) to BTC and MSTR.
